 Advertisement Pineapple express brings potentially historic flooding to Southwest
 A weather system is soaking the Desert Southwest, with mandatory evacuations and potentially historic flooding.
 By Jonathan Erdman and Rob Shackelford • 11 hours ago Updated: November 1, 2026, 2:49 pm EST Published: November 1, 2026, 7:31 am EST Share Share
 1 . Where is the soaking rain? Chevron Down 
 An atmospheric river referred to as the "pineapple express" is bringing heavy rain to parts of the Desert Southwest and Southern California, just over a week after destructive flooding plagued parts of Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico and Utah.
 These atmospheric rivers often fuel heavy rain events in the West, especially in a stronger El Niño winter. 
 We'll discuss more about this pattern after laying out the important forecast details.

 Where is the soaking rain?
 A large batch of precipitation is ramping up and spreading further into the West. You can see current radar, watches, and warnings in the map above.
 Mandatory evacuations are ongoing in parts of Sedona, Arizona near Oak Creek, as well as parts of Archuleta County, near Pagosa Springs, Colorado. The San Juan River is forecast to crest as high as 20 feet late Sunday night, breaking historic records.

 The heaviest rain is the red locations on the map below. While Phoenix just misses this region, it is still in the level 2 of 4 threat on this map. Flagstaff, Arizona; Zion National Park, Utah and pockets of northern New Mexico and southern Colorado could see the greatest rainfall and rainfall rates. 
 What are the potential impacts?
 A more serious flash flood threat is in play for the Desert Southwest, but there will be some concern for wintry weather, too. Below are the current flood and winter weather alerts. 
 Current alerts for winter weather and flooding
 The ground is still saturated from the 2 to 5 inches of rain that soaked the area last week, triggering major flash flooding in northern Arizona , New Mexico, southern Colorado and southern Utah . 
 The map below shows total additional rainfall in the Southwest. Areas shaded in darker green and yellow could see more dangerous, widespread flash flooding. 
 The areas of greatest concern are:
 Elevations below snow level in southwestern Colorado and the immediate Four Corners area
 The Phoenix metro's north and east sides and the Mogollon Rim of northern Arizona
 The canyonlands of southern Utah
 Any ground scorched by recent wildfires, which is particularly susceptible to producing fast-moving debris flows, rock and mudslides, even in modest rainfall. 
 According to the National Weather Service in Flagstaff, Arizona, rivers such as the Little Colorado and Verde, could run high for days after this weekend's latest soaking.
 Over the higher elevations, this precipitation may fall as snow over the higher peaks of the Rockies and Sierra. This may lead to slippery travel mainly Sunday into Monday over mountain passes. 
 What's fueling this soaking?
 What's fueling this soaking is a southward plunge of the jet stream near the West Coast. 
 That jet stream will pull a ribbon of deep tropical moisture called an atmospheric river into the Southwest. 
 This particular atmospheric river tap is originating from near Hawaii, something meteorologists nickname the "pineapple express."
 This is the forecast weather pattern for Halloween weekend, showing an atmospheric river headed into California and the Southwest.
 It's not a strong version of either an atmospheric river or pineapple express, but the moisture fueling this heavy rain could be record-setting for this time of year.
 This could be a harbinger, given the tendency for a wetter Southwest during most stronger El Niños from fall through spring. 
 Jonathan Erdman is a senior meteorologist at weather.com and has been covering national and international weather since 1996. Extreme and bizarre weather are his favorite topics. Reach out to him on Bluesky , X (formerly Twitter) and Facebook .
